Knowing what you're feeling

by the Sky System, Ellis of the Pleiadesfolk

Not knowing what you’re feeling can be a real bitch.

Emotions can often feel… difficult. At times, it might feel like something you have to perform, in response to things that are going on around you. You might be expected to laugh at a joke. You might be told that you need to be angry. You might have to pretend that you’re surprised. You might expect to feel icky but just not have any feeling at all. You might be expected to feel grief after a loss and yet feel nothing.

It’s a pretty common condition named alexithymia, and it can be very disorienting. Alexithymia — described as a relative constriction in emotional functioning (i.e. a loss in emotional function) and an inability to find the words to describe emotions. You don’t know how exactly to describe the emotion you’re feeling, and you can’t identify them.

Autistic people experience alexithymia at a higher rate, and the condition is also more common with people who have OCD, PTSD, anxiety and depression. Says Rebecca Ellis (no relation with the Pleiadesfolk):

Alexithymia affects how a person experiences and interprets emotions, from noticing physical sensations in the body, to identifying them as specific feelings and deciding how to respond.

(…) Someone with alexithymia may need to look back at an event to understand what they were feeling at the particular moment through contextual clues. They often adapt their actions to cope with this in future situations.

Knowing how you feel can be important in many situations — it can help you understand yourself, respond appropriately to others, and learn how to process these emotions. Emotional regulation might also become more challenging if you can’t identify how you feel, and so will emotional responses in a social situation — people might find attempts to reason through and interpret your emotional response as awkward or abnormal, or worse, as a lack of character.

We (the Pleiadesfolk) were dissociated to heck before we transitioned. We lived life in a haze, but there was always this quaint light within us — the light that we now know as Riley, perhaps — that drove us to be kind, to love.

So we’ve always sort of felt this lack. The fact that we were not attuned to our emotions meant that we were often accused of being emotionally unintelligent. In effect we were gifted many self-help books to help us with that, since it was something that we regularly complained about not being good at.

We the Pleiadesfolk aren’t alone in this. Says the Sky System:

For us, alexithymia ranges from “I can tell I’m feeling a positive/negative emotion, but I can’t tell what it is” to “I can tell that I’m feeling something and that’s all”, to “I’m not even sure I have feelings”, to “I can’t connect these emotions to the event that caused them because it took me so long to notice I was feeling it” to “I unconsciously escalate situations because I need a feeling to be very intense to know it’s there”

It can also depend on which headmate’s fronting.

Post-transition, we the Pleiadesfolk have come to understand that some headmates are just closer to emotion than others. Some parts of us may be prone to anger, for instance. Others are closer to joy, perhaps. Notably, early in our syscovery, we found a part of us that had one simple role: to determine what we were supposed to feel in the moment. That internal self-helper — T’lyn, named after the Star Trek: Lower Decks character — had been essential in helping us through that one time we were in an Large Group Awareness Training cult program.
